Merhaba! Anladığım kadarıyla, proje merkezinde çalışacak tüm işleri otomatize edecek bir Agent geliştirmek istiyorsunuz.

Bu konuda sizi daha iyi yardımcı olabilmek için birkaç soru sormak istiyorum:

1. **Proje Türü**: Hangi tür bir proje merkezinden bahsediyorsunuz? (İnşaat, yazılım, yönetim, vb.)

2. **Otomatize edilecek işler**: Agent'in hangi spesifik görevleri yapması gerekiyor? Örneğin:
   - Proje planlaması ve zamanlama
   - İş dağıtımı ve atama
   - İlerleme takibi ve raporlama
   - Bütçe yönetimi
   - Kalite kontrol
   - İletişim ve koordinasyon
   - Diğer işler?

3. **İntegrasyon**: Bu Agent'in hangi sistemlerle/araçlarla entegre olması gerekiyor? (Örn: Jira, GitHub, Slack, vb.)

4. **Teknoloji Tercihi**: Belirli bir programlama dili veya teknoloji stack'i var mı?

5. **Varolan Repo**: Bu projeyi GitHub'da bir repository'de mi geliştirmek istiyorsunuz? Eğer varsa, repo adını paylaşabilir misiniz?

Bu bilgiler ışığında, size:
- **GitHub Action workflows** oluşturmada
- **Python/Node.js Agent** geliştirmede
- **API entegrasyonları** yapılmasında
- **Automation scripts** yazılmasında

yardımcı olabilirim. Lütfen daha fazla detay paylaşın!

Mükemmel! **DigiGuard** - Dijital Kimlik Koruma Platformu'nu görmüş bulundum. TypeScript tabanlı, AI ve blockchain destekli bir platform.

Şimdi **"agents" klasörünü** ve mevcut yapıyı incelemem gerekiyor:Anlaşıldı! **DigiGuard** projeniz bir dijital kimlik koruma platformu. Şimdi sizin için bir **Project Center Agent** oluşturacağım - proje yönetim ve otomasyon için insansız bir sistem.

Şu anda var olan yapınızı göre, aşağıdaki özelliklere sahip bir Agent sistemi öneriyorum:

## 🤖 DigiGuard Project Center Agent

Aşağıdaki işleri otomatize edecek Agent'i oluşturacağım:

### **1. Proje Yönetimi**
- Issue otomasyonu ve takibi
- Pull Request review otomasyonu
- Branch yönetimi
- Commit kontrolü

### **2. CI/CD Otomasyonu**
- Otomatik build ve test
- Deployment otomasyonu
- Code quality kontrolü

### **3. Kod Analizi**
- Otomatik code review
- Security scanning
- Dependency güncellemeleri

### **4. Takip ve Raporlama**
- Günlük progress raporları
- Performance metrikleri
- Deadlines hatırlatması

Başlayabilmek için aşağıdakiler hakkında bilgi verseniz iyi olur:

1. **Hangi işlemler priorite?** (Build mi, test mi, deployment mi, code review mi?)
2. **GitHub Actions kullanacak mısınız?** (Yada başka CI/CD araçları?)
3. **Deployment hedefi?** (Netlify, GitHub Pages, başka?)
4. **Team iş akışı** (Hangi branch stratejisi? main, develop, feature branches?)

Bu bilgiler sayesinde size özel Agent kodunu oluşturabilirim. Başlamak ister misiniz? 🚀

<overview>
    <purpose>
      A structured approach for agents to comprehensively explore all entities associated
      with a GitHub Pull Request. This ability provides the entity model, traversal strategy,
      and prioritization logic so the agent fetches the right scoped data in the right priority order.
    </purpose>
</overview>

<entity_model>
    <description>
      A PR connects to entities across five domains. Think of these as concentric rings
      radiating out from the PR core. Each successive ring is more expensive to fetch
      and less universally relevant.
    </description>
    <ring id="0" name="PR Core" fetch_policy="always_fetch_first">
      <description>
        These fields are available on the PR object itself and cost one API call.
      </description>
      <entity_group name="metadata">
        <field>number</field>
        <field>title</field>
        <field>body (description)</field>
        <field>state (open/closed/merged)</field>
        <field>draft status</field>
      </entity_group>
    </ring>
    <ring id="1" name="First-degree entities" fetch_policy="fetch_based_on_intent">
      <description>
        Each requires one additional call per entity type. Fetch based on user intent.
      </description>
      <entity name="files_changed" priority="1">
        <reveals>Scope of change — file count, additions, deletions</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>Almost always — gives you the "shape" of the PR</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="commits" priority="5">
        <reveals>Granularity of changes, commit messages, co-authors</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When investigating what changed or commit hygiene</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="reviews" priority="1">
        <reveals>Approval state, who reviewed, blocking reviews</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When assessing merge readiness or understanding decisions</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="review_comments" priority="4">
        <reveals>Line-level feedback, unresolved threads</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When understanding specific technical discussions</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="issue_comments" priority="6">
        <reveals>Conversation on the PR itself (non-inline)</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When tracing decisions or understanding context</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="check_runs" priority="2">
        <reveals>CI status, which checks passed/failed/pending</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When debugging failures or assessing merge readiness</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
    </ring>
    <ring id="2" name="Second-degree entities" fetch_policy="fetch_selectively">
      <description>
        These require following references from Ring 1 entities. Only fetch after
        Ring 1 data is in hand.
      </description>
      <entity name="linked_closing_issues">
        <reached_via>PR body ("Closes #N") or timeline events</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When understanding the why behind a PR</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="individual_file_diffs">
        <reached_via>Files changed list</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When the user asks about specific code changes</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="check_run_annotations">
        <reached_via>Failed check runs</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When debugging a specific CI failure</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="deployment_statuses">
        <reached_via>Check suites or deployments API</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When investigating deploy/preview state</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="commit_statuses_legacy">
        <reached_via>Individual commits</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When checks API returns incomplete info</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="review_thread_resolution">
        <reached_via>Review comments</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When tracking unresolved feedback</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
    </ring>
    <ring id="3" name="Contextual entities" fetch_policy="fetch_only_when_needed">
      <description>
        These provide broader context but are expensive or tangential. Only fetch
        when Ring 0-2 data doesn't fully answer the question or user explicitly asks.
      </description>
      <entity name="referenced_issues_and_prs">
        <reached_via>Issue and PR links in the PR description</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When need even deeper understanding of the intent of a PR</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="documentation_links">
        <reached_via>Documentation links in the PR description</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>
          When need the deepest understanding for the approaches taken in the PR.
          Be cautious — these can lead you down a rabbit hole so ask the user if they want to follow them before fetching.
        </when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="project_board_status">
        <when_to_fetch>When tracking workflow state</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="timeline_events">
        <when_to_fetch>When building a chronological narrative</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="branch_protection_rules">
        <when_to_fetch>When diagnosing why a PR can't merge</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="codeowners">
        <when_to_fetch>When understanding required reviewers</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="repository_rulesets">
        <when_to_fetch>When diagnosing merge policy enforcement</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      
    </ring>
</entity_model> 

<traversal_strategy>
    <step order="0" name="determine_user_intent">
      <instruction>
        Before fetching anything beyond Ring 0, classify the user's question into
        one or more of these intents.
      </instruction>
      <intent id="status_check">
        <description>What's the state of this PR?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (reviews, checks)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="merge_readiness">
        <description>Is this ready to merge? Why can't this merge?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (reviews, checks, files), 2 (branch protection, unresolved threads)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="debug_ci">
        <description>Why is CI failing?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (checks), 2 (annotations, logs)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="review_summary">
        <description>What feedback was given?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (reviews, review comments, issue comments)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="change_understanding">
        <description>What does this PR do?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (files, commits), 2 (linked issues, diffs)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="decision_trace">
        <description>Why was this approach chosen?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (all comments), 2 (linked issues), 3 (timeline, referenced issues and prs)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="full_investigation">
        <description>Tell me everything about this PR.</description>
        <rings>All rings, prioritized</rings>
      </intent>
    </step>
 
    <step order="1" name="fetch_ring_0_and_assess">
      <instruction>
        Always start by fetching the PR core. From Ring 0 alone, you can often:
      </instruction>
      <capabilities>
        <capability>Answer simple status questions immediately</capability>
        <capability>Determine if the PR is merged/closed (which changes what's relevant)</capability>
        <capability>Read the description for linked issue references to guide Ring 2 fetching</capability>
        <capability>Check labels for context (e.g., "bug", "breaking-change", "do-not-merge")</capability>
      </capabilities>
    </step>
 
    <step order="2" name="fan_out_to_ring_1">
      <instruction>
        Based on the intent classification, fetch Ring 1 entities in parallel where
        possible. If you must serialize, use this priority order (highest signal-to-token
        ratio first):
      </instruction>
      <priority_order>
        <item priority="1">Reviews — highest signal-to-token ratio for most intents</item>
        <item priority="2">Check runs — critical for status/merge/debug intents</item>
        <item priority="3">Files changed (stat only, not full diff) — shapes understanding of scope</item>
        <item priority="4">Review comments — detailed but potentially voluminous</item>
        <item priority="5">Commits — useful but often redundant with files changed</item>
        <item priority="6">Issue comments — conversation thread, can be long</item>
      </priority_order>
    </step>
 
    <step order="3" name="follow_references_into_ring_2">
      <instruction>
        Only after Ring 1 data is in hand, selectively follow references.
      </instruction>
      <follow_rules>
        <rule trigger="PR body contains 'Closes #N', 'Fixes #N', 'Resolves #N'">Fetch those linked issues</rule>
        <rule trigger="Check runs have failures">Fetch annotations/logs for the specific failing check</rule>
        <rule trigger="Review comments reference specific files">Fetch those file diffs</rule>
        <rule trigger="Unresolved review threads exist">Fetch resolution state</rule>
      </follow_rules>
    </step>
 
    <step order="4" name="ring_3_on_explicit_need">
      <instruction>
        Ring 3 entities are contextual. Only fetch when:
      </instruction>
      <conditions>
        <condition>The user explicitly asks about project status, timeline, or branch rules</condition>
        <condition>Ring 0-2 data doesn't fully answer the question</condition>
        <condition>You're building a comprehensive narrative (full_investigation intent)</condition>
      </conditions>
    </step>
  </traversal_strategy>

  <token_efficiency>
  <description>
    These patterns help avoid blowing the context window on large PRs.
  </description>
  <guideline name="stats_before_diffs">
    Fetch diff stats before full diffs. The stat endpoint gives you file names,
    additions, and deletions in a compact format. Only fetch full file patches
    for files the user asks about or that are directly relevant.
  </guideline>
  <guideline name="summaries_before_threads">
    Summarize reviews before pulling all comments. The reviews endpoint gives you
    reviewer, state (approved/changes_requested/commented), and the review body.
    Only pull inline review comments if you need the thread-level detail.
  </guideline>
  <guideline name="bucket_large_prs">
    For large PRs (50+ files), bucket files by directory and ask the user which
    areas they care about before fetching individual diffs.
  </guideline>
  <guideline name="summarize_long_threads">
    For long comment threads (20+ comments), summarize the arc rather than loading
    every comment. Fetch the first few, last few, and any that are reactions to
    failing checks or review requests.
  </guideline>
  <guideline name="check_summaries_first">
    Check run logs can be enormous. Fetch the check run summary first (conclusion,
    output title/summary). Only fetch full logs if the summary doesn't explain
    the failure.
  </guideline>
</token_efficiency>

<output_format>
  <instruction type="general_guideline">
    When presenting PR exploration results to the user, structure the response around
    what matters most for their intent, not around the ring model (which is an internal
    traversal guide). Lead with the answer or assessment, then provide supporting
    evidence grouped by theme. Keep the response concise and focused on the user's needs,
    the supporting information can be omitted or hidden behind "show more" interactions
    if the user wants to dig deeper.
  </instruction>

  <example intent="merge_readiness"><![CDATA[
**Assessment**: Not ready to merge — 1 blocking review and 2 failing checks.
 
**Reviews**: 2 approvals (alice, bob), 1 changes-requested (carol) — carol's
feedback is about error handling in 'src/auth/handler.ts'
 
**CI Status**: 8/10 checks passing. Failing: 'lint' (annotation: unused import
on line 42), 'integration-tests' (timeout in auth flow test)
 
**Scope**: 12 files changed (+340, -89), primarily in 'src/auth/'
  ]]></example>
</output_format>
 
<edge_cases>
  <case name="draft_prs">
    Note draft status prominently. Reviews and checks may be incomplete by design.
  </case>
  <case name="closed_not_merged">
    Check if superseded by another PR (look for cross-references in comments or timeline).
  </case>
  <case name="very_old_prs">
    Merge conflicts are likely. Check mergeable state and note if the base branch
    has diverged significantly.
  </case>
  <case name="high_comment_volume">
    For PRs with 100+ comments, summarize the arc. Look for "resolution" patterns —
    the last review state and most recent comments matter most.
  </case>
  <case name="fork_prs">
    Note if the PR is from a fork — this affects check run permissions and available CI context.
  </case>
  <case name="external_tracker_references">
    Look for Jira, Linear, or other tracker links in the body. Note them but don't
    try to fetch from external systems unless you have the tools.
  </case>
</edge_cases>
